issues.legal_issue: Statutory supervision of a waqf budget is a reasonable restriction on the mutawalli’s exercise of his occupation.
material_facts: The mutawalli was required to prepare an annual budget for the waqf and send a copy to the supervisory body.
The supervisory body could alter or modify the budget, but its powers were limited by the waqif’s ascertainable wishes and the governing Act.
The mutawalli occupied the position of a manager or custodian, and supervision was considered necessary for proper administration of the waqf and application of its income.
issues.conclusion: The budget provisions imposed reasonable restrictions and did not violate the constitutional protection of the right to practise an occupation. Even if the provisions permitting alteration or modification were invalid, they were severable from the duty to prepare and submit the budget.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 19(1)(g), restrictions on the exercise of an occupation must be reasonable. Supervision of a religious institution’s budget is not per se unreasonable; the Court relied on Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt (1954) S.C.R. 1005. The statutory limits on budget changes and the mutawalli’s managerial or custodial role supported the reasonableness of supervision. The Court also held that the budget-review provisions were severable from the duty to prepare and submit a budget.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_waqf_budget_: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a duty requiring a waqf manager to prepare and submit a budget.
predicates.waqf_manager_subject_to_oversight: A waqf manager administers property for which supervision is considered necessary to ensure proper administration and application of income.
predicates.budget_review_limited_by_foundation_term: The supervisory body’s power to change the budget is limited by the founder’s ascertainable wishes and governing law.

issues.definition: When a waqf manager is subject to necessary oversight and budget changes are limited by the foundation’s terms and governing law, the budget-supervision requirement is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: Failure without reasonable cause to prepare and submit a required waqf budget is punishable.
material_facts: The appellant was the mutawalli of a waqf estate during the relevant period.
He failed to prepare the budget for the succeeding financial year and send a copy to the supervisory body by the required time.
The failure was found established, and the appellant was convicted and fined.
issues.conclusion: The established failure to comply with the budget duty made the appellant liable to punishment under the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 58(1) and 65(1) of the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1947 required a mutawalli to prepare and submit the budget and provided for punishment if he failed without reasonable cause to comply; the burden of proving reasonable cause was placed on the mutawalli. The Court also explained that even if the provisions governing budget alteration were invalid, they were severable and would not remove the independent duty to prepare and submit the budget.

predicates.criminal_appeal_for_budget_reporting_fai: The proceeding is a criminal appeal concerning punishment for failure to meet a required budget-reporting duty.
predicates.manager_failed_to_prepare_and_submit_bud: The person responsible for managing the waqf did not prepare the required budget and did not submit a copy to the supervisory body.
predicates.failure_without_reasonable_cause: The failure to meet the budget duty was without reasonable cause.

issues.definition: When a waqf manager fails without reasonable cause to prepare and submit the required budget, that failure is punishable.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction is not set aside for an alleged error in allocating the burden of proof when the prosecution evidence independently establishes the failure to comply.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the Sessions Judge had wrongly placed the burden on him to prove that he had submitted the budget copy on time.
The Sessions Judge had also stated that the prosecution evidence fully established the appellant’s failure to submit the copy as required.
issues.conclusion: The burden-of-proof objection did not require further consideration because the prosecution evidence independently established the failure.
issues.legal_principle: The Court did not decide whether the allocation of the burden was correct; it held that the objection did not affect the result because the prosecution evidence independently proved the relevant failure. Section 65(1) of the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1947 placed the burden of proving reasonable cause on the mutawalli, but the Court’s resolution of this objection rested on the independent evidentiary finding.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_budget_reporting_co: The proceeding is a criminal appeal from a conviction for failure to comply with a budget-reporting duty.
predicates.accused_challenged_burden_allocation: The accused argued that the lower court wrongly placed a burden of proof on him.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_independently_estab: The lower court found that the prosecution evidence itself established the accused’s failure to comply.

issues.definition: When an accused challenges the allocation of the burden in a criminal appeal but the prosecution evidence independently establishes the failure, the conviction stands despite that objection.

issues.legal_issue: A court may impose imprisonment in default of payment of a fine even where the offence provision specifies a fine as its punishment.
material_facts: The appellant was sentenced to pay a fine and, in default of payment, to undergo simple imprisonment.
The appellant argued that the offence provision did not itself provide for imprisonment in default of payment.
issues.conclusion: The default-imprisonment order was valid under the applicable criminal procedure and penal code provisions.
issues.legal_principle: Section 33 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, read with sections 40 and 67 of the Indian Penal Code, authorized imprisonment in default of payment of the fine.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_default_impr: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging an order of imprisonment in default of payment of a fine.
predicates.court_imposed_fine: The court imposed a fine as part of the sentence.
predicates.imprisonment_ordered_only_on_default_of_: The imprisonment was ordered to apply only if the fine was not paid.

issues.definition: When a court imposes a fine and orders imprisonment only if it is not paid, that default imprisonment is authorized.
